study.title: Psalm 1 - Two paths, two destinations
study.overview: Psalm 1 opens the psaltery as a sapiential invitation: it presents, in a very direct way, two ways of living and its results. There is the way of the righteous, marked by the separation from sin, delight in the instruction of the Lord and fruitful perseverance; and there is the way of the wicked, which seems strong for a time, but ends in dispersion, inability to stand before judgment and perishment. The Psalm teaches that human life is morally guided by choices, habits and inner direction, and that the Lord sees, sustains and approves the way of the righteous.

outline.title: The path of the just is defined by separation and delight
outline.explanation: The text begins with a bliss: the happiness of man who does not mold himself to the counsel of the wicked, is not fixed in the way of sinners and does not sit with the scoffers. The movement is progressive: advice, path and seat suggest influence, practice and belonging. In contrast, the righteous finds pleasure in the law of the Lord and meditates it continually. The notes point out that divine instruction is the complete revelation of God's commandments and that meditating on it involves constant inner reflection at all times.

outline.title: The righteous is fertile; the ungodly is light and unmandaent
outline.explanation: The image of the tree near the waters describes stability, nutrition and fertility. The righteous not only survives, but bears fruit in the right time; his life has vitality and continuity. The evil ones are compared to the straw carried by the wind, image of fragility and emptiness. Therefore, when the judgment arrives, they do not remain: they are unable to endure the assessment of God and remain outside the assembly of the righteous.

outline.title: The Lord knows the way of the righteous
outline.explanation: The closure of the psalm summarizes the decisive difference between the two paths. The Lord knows the way of the righteous, that is, not only knows it in an abstract way, but recognizes it, approves it and guards. But the way of the wicked will perish: their plans, their direction, and their end, do not stand before divine justice.

study.context: By the notes provided, this psalm functions as an introduction to the book of Psalms, and Tyndale's notes read it in relation to Psalms 1 and 2 as an opening that contrasts wisdom and rebellion. The focus of the psalm itself, however, is less in historical detail and more in moral and spiritual teaching: it presents the ideal of the godly man and the ruin of the wicked. The notes also note that the theme of psalm is the instruction of the Lord and the contrast between the path leading to life and what leads to destruction.
study.theology: Theologically, the psalm teaches that life before God is guided by two irreconcilable paths. Happiness is not born of moral autonomy, but from loving submission to the instruction of the Lord. Continuous meditation in the law is not mere intellectual exercise; it is a way to align desires, thoughts, and actions to the character of God. The figure of the tree shows that piety produces lasting fruit, not necessarily visible success in human terms, but firmness, usefulness and perseverance. The psalm also affirms the reality of judgment: the wicked cannot stand before the divine assessment. Finally, the phrase about the Lord knowing the way of the righteous points to divine providence, approval and preservation, while the end of the way of the wicked shows the seriousness of moral retribution. Tyndale's notes relate this to the Lord's principle of retribution, and Adam Clarke's notes reinforce the idea that the Lord approves and guards the righteous. These readings are interpretative, but they are in harmony with the explicit contrast of the text.

scholarViews.insight: The image of the well irrigated tree shows that the righteous persevere and produce abundant fruit, because they live nourished by the instruction of the Lord.
The psalm clearly describes two groups and puts them before life and death, blessing and curse, so that each person will examine his own way.
Meditation in the law is not occasional, but constant, and the blessed man brings his affections and actions to this holy rule.

questions: What influences today more shape my counsel, my habits and my place of belonging: the way of the righteous or the evil?
Is my relationship with the Word only informative, or does it involve delight and continuous meditation that guides my decisions?
What kind of fruit is my life producing, and this fruit points to stability in God or to transient fragility?
study.practice: Choose a concrete practice for this week: to separate daily a fixed time to read a biblical passage, meditate on it in silence and turn into prayer a practical application. At the same time, identify a harmful influence - advice, environment or habit - and take a clear step to avoid it. Finally, seek to produce a visible fruit of the Word in a concrete attitude of justice, truth or mercy.
study.uncertainty: The notes provided do not detail the historical context of the psalm, and this study avoids affirming elements not explicitly supported by them. Some cited comments offer confessional or expanded readings, such as connections with the rest of the psaltery and applications on judgment and retribution; these readings were treated as interpretations, not as closed definitions of the text.
